stem: What was the League of Nations’ mandate system intended to do after the First World War?

options.text: Place former German and Ottoman territories under administration by an approved power pending development toward self-government
Restore the German colonies directly to Germany
Create independent states immediately in every former empire
Transfer all territories to the United States

explanation: The mandate system placed former German and Ottoman territories under administration by other powers, formally under League oversight.

stem: Which organisation formally supervised the mandate system?

options.text: North Atlantic Treaty Organization
League of Nations
European Union
United Nations Security Council

explanation: The League of Nations was responsible for supervising the mandate system established after the war.

stem: Which statement best describes the mandate system?

options.text: It made every mandated territory a province of the United States
It immediately granted full independence to all former colonies
It assigned administration of former imperial territories to powers under international oversight
It restored the prewar German colonial empire

explanation: The League’s mandate system placed territories under administering powers while claiming international oversight; the path to self-government varied.

stem: Which region included former Ottoman territories placed under British or French mandates after the war?

options.text: Scandinavia
The Low Countries
The Caribbean
The Middle East

explanation: Former Ottoman territories in the Middle East were assigned to British and French administration under the mandate system.

stem: Why is it inaccurate to describe the postwar mandates as immediate independence for former colonies?

options.text: They were administered by outside powers under League supervision rather than becoming sovereign states at once
The League abolished all colonial administrations in 1919
The territories became part of Germany again
They were governed by elected global assemblies with full sovereignty

explanation: Mandates remained under external administration and did not grant immediate sovereign independence.

stem: Which statement about postwar territorial settlements is accurate?

options.text: They restored every European border to its 1914 position
The settlements changed borders and placed some former imperial territories under mandates
They created a single state from all former Ottoman lands
They ended all disputes over national self-determination

explanation: The postwar settlement redrew borders and created mandates, but it did not resolve every national or territorial dispute.

stem: What was the League of Nations created to promote?

options.text: A single European army under German command
The restoration of the Habsburg Empire
International cooperation and collective security
Colonial competition among its members

explanation: The League was intended to provide a forum for cooperation and collective security after the war.

stem: Which major power did not join the League of Nations despite President Wilson’s support for it?

options.text: France
Britain
Japan
The United States

explanation: The U.S. Senate did not ratify the Treaty of Versailles, and the United States never joined the League.

stem: What did collective security mean in the League’s stated principles?

options.text: Members would cooperate to respond to aggression and protect peace
Each state would pursue security only through colonies
The League would guarantee every member victory in war
Members would avoid all international negotiations

explanation: Collective security relied on members acting together against threats to peace, but the League lacked reliable enforcement power.

stem: Which body was included in the League of Nations’ institutional structure?

options.text: The European Parliament
The Assembly
The Security Council of the United Nations
The Warsaw Pact Secretariat

explanation: The League’s structure included an Assembly and a Council, along with a permanent Secretariat.

stem: Which limitation weakened the League’s ability to stop aggression?

options.text: It had authority over every national army
It could automatically compel the United States to join
It had no standing military force and depended on member states to act
It controlled all colonial administrations directly

explanation: The League relied on its members for sanctions and enforcement and had no independent military force.

stem: Why did the League’s failure to include the United States matter?

options.text: It prevented France and Britain from joining
It automatically dissolved the League in 1919
It made the mandate system illegal
It weakened the organisation’s reach and the collective security system Wilson had promoted

explanation: U.S. non-membership weakened the League’s political weight and limited the collective security framework.

stem: What happened when Japan rejected the League’s criticism of its actions in Manchuria?

options.text: Japan withdrew from the League in 1933
Japan became a permanent League military commander
The League transferred Manchuria to Germany
China left the League and joined the Axis

explanation: Japan announced its withdrawal from the League after the organisation criticised its actions in Manchuria.

stem: Which event exposed the limits of collective security in East Asia during the early 1930s?

options.text: The League’s successful disarmament of Japan
Japan’s occupation of Manchuria after the Mukden Incident and the League’s inability to reverse it
The transfer of Manchuria to China by a League army
The creation of the United Nations in 1931

explanation: The League condemned Japanese actions, but could not compel Japan to withdraw from Manchuria.

stem: Which proposal formed part of the League of Nations Covenant?

options.text: All members had to abolish their governments
Every dispute had to be settled by the U.S. Congress
Members were to respect one another’s territorial integrity and political independence
Colonies were to be divided equally among League members

explanation: The Covenant included commitments concerning members’ territorial integrity and political independence.

stem: Which conclusion about the League of Nations is most accurate?

options.text: It had no role in diplomacy or mandates
It controlled a permanent army that defeated every aggressor
It ended international conflict throughout the interwar period
It created a forum and collective security rules, but lacked the unity and enforcement capacity to stop determined aggressors

explanation: The League developed institutions and rules, but political divisions and reliance on member action limited its effectiveness.

stem: Which constitution established the Weimar Republic in Germany?

options.text: The constitution adopted in 1919
The German Basic Law of 1949
The Constitution of 1871 unchanged
The Treaty of Rome

explanation: The Weimar Constitution was adopted in 1919 and established Germany’s postwar republic.

stem: What was the German national parliament under the Weimar Constitution called?

options.text: The Bundestag
The Reichstag
The Duma
The Estates-General

explanation: The Reichstag was the elected national parliament of the Weimar Republic.

stem: Which feature of the Weimar Constitution gave the president emergency powers?

options.text: Article 10 of the League Covenant
The Enabling Act of 1933
Article 48
The Munich Agreement

explanation: Article 48 allowed the president to take emergency measures under specified conditions; its use became politically significant.

stem: Which economic crisis struck Germany especially severely in 1923?

options.text: The oil crisis
The Great Depression
The European debt crisis of 2010
Hyperinflation

explanation: Germany experienced severe hyperinflation in 1923, eroding the value of the mark and savings.

stem: Which plan helped stabilise the German economy in the mid-1920s?

options.text: The Dawes Plan
The Schlieffen Plan
The Marshall Plan
The Young Italy programme

explanation: The Dawes Plan of 1924 restructured reparations payments and helped stabilise the German economy, with reliance on U.S. loans.

stem: Which statement best characterises the Weimar Republic before the Great Depression?

options.text: It had no elected institutions at any point
It experienced serious crises but also periods of relative recovery; its collapse was not inevitable
It was a Nazi dictatorship from 1919
It remained economically stable throughout the 1920s

explanation: Weimar Germany faced major crises and also achieved periods of recovery; historians do not treat its collapse as inevitable.

stem: Which political system did the Weimar Constitution establish?

options.text: An absolute monarchy under the Hohenzollerns
A military government controlled by the League
A parliamentary republic with an elected Reichstag and a president
A federal empire ruled by Austria

explanation: The 1919 constitution established a republic with parliamentary institutions and an elected president.

stem: How did proportional representation affect Weimar politics?

options.text: It banned all parties except the Social Democrats
It gave the League the right to appoint the Reichstag
It ensured a permanent majority for one party
It allowed smaller parties to gain seats and could make stable parliamentary coalitions difficult

explanation: Proportional representation allowed a range of parties to win seats, contributing to coalition politics; it was one factor among several in political instability.

stem: When did the Great Depression begin?

options.text: After the 1929 financial crash
After the 1914 assassination at Sarajevo
After the 1918 armistice
After the 1939 invasion of Poland

explanation: The global economic downturn began after the 1929 crash and spread internationally.

stem: Why was Germany especially vulnerable when U.S. lending contracted after 1929?

options.text: It had no industrial economy
Its recovery had depended heavily on foreign loans, including American credit
It had already left the League of Nations
It received no loans during the 1920s

explanation: Germany’s mid-1920s recovery relied significantly on foreign credit, making the withdrawal of U.S. loans damaging.

stem: Which condition increased sharply in Germany during the Great Depression?

options.text: Colonial exports to Germany
The value of the mark during hyperinflation
Unemployment
Membership in the League of Nations

explanation: The Depression brought mass unemployment and economic hardship to Germany.

stem: How did the Great Depression affect politics in Germany?

options.text: It immediately restored the monarchy
It ended all political violence
It removed the Reichstag from the constitution
Economic hardship helped increase support for radical parties, including the Nazis

explanation: The Depression intensified hardship and helped radical parties gain support, though it was not the only cause of Nazi growth.

stem: Which explanation best describes the relationship between the Depression and Nazi support?

options.text: The crisis contributed to Nazi gains, but earlier political, social and institutional factors also mattered
The Depression alone created the Nazi Party in 1929
The Depression had no effect on German politics
The Nazis lost all support during the crisis

explanation: The Depression was an important contributing factor, but Nazi growth also reflected earlier developments and political choices.

stem: Which global effect followed the Great Depression?

options.text: All states abandoned tariffs and achieved full employment
Contraction in trade and production spread hardship across many countries
The crisis remained limited to Germany
Industrial output increased uniformly worldwide

explanation: The downturn spread through international finance and trade, with effects that varied among countries.

stem: Who founded the Italian Fascist movement and became prime minister in 1922?

options.text: Adolf Hitler
Francisco Franco
Benito Mussolini
Vladimir Lenin

explanation: Mussolini founded the Fascist movement and was appointed prime minister in October 1922.

stem: Which event preceded Mussolini’s appointment as prime minister in 1922?

options.text: The Munich Agreement
The Mukden Incident
The Beer Hall Putsch of 1923
The March on Rome

explanation: The Fascist March on Rome took place in October 1922; King Victor Emmanuel III then appointed Mussolini prime minister.

stem: Who appointed Adolf Hitler chancellor of Germany in January 1933?

options.text: President Paul von Hindenburg
Kaiser Wilhelm II
Benito Mussolini
The League of Nations Assembly

explanation: Hindenburg appointed Hitler chancellor on 30 January 1933.

stem: Which party did Adolf Hitler lead in Germany?

options.text: The Italian Socialist Party
The National Socialist German Workers’ Party (Nazi Party)
The German Centre Party
The Spartacist League

explanation: Hitler led the Nazi Party, which gained support in the political crises of the Weimar era.

stem: Which ideology did Mussolini lead in Italy?

options.text: Bolshevism
Chartism
Fascism
Liberal internationalism

explanation: Mussolini was the leading figure of Italian Fascism, an authoritarian nationalist movement.

stem: Which statement about Hitler’s rise to power is accurate?

options.text: He seized the presidency in a direct popular election in 1933
He was appointed by the League of Nations
He became chancellor before the Nazi Party existed
He was appointed chancellor through a political decision and then used state power to dismantle democracy

explanation: Hitler was appointed chancellor by Hindenburg; the Nazis then consolidated power through political manoeuvres, legislation, coercion and propaganda.

stem: What did the Reichstag Fire Decree of February 1933 enable the Nazi regime to do?

options.text: Suspend civil liberties and intensify repression of political opponents
Restore the Weimar constitution’s checks on emergency powers
End the Nazi Party’s control of the police
Transfer Germany’s colonies to the League

explanation: The decree suspended key civil liberties and enabled arrests and repression after the Reichstag fire.

stem: What did the Enabling Act of March 1933 allow Hitler’s government to do?

options.text: Restore the monarchy under Wilhelm II
Pass laws without the Reichstag, including laws that could depart from the constitution
Give the League control of German courts
End the Nazi government’s legislative authority

explanation: The Enabling Act gave Hitler’s cabinet legislative power, undermining parliamentary government.

stem: Which method did the Nazi regime use to consolidate control?

options.text: Regular peaceful transfers of power to opposition parties
Abolition of police and censorship
A combination of legislation, coercion, propaganda and institutional changes
Transfer of government authority to the League of Nations

explanation: The Nazi regime combined legal changes with violence, propaganda and institutional control to destroy opposition.

stem: Which statement about the Nazi seizure of power is best supported?

options.text: Hitler won an outright majority in a presidential election and immediately abolished every law
The League appointed Hitler to lead Germany
The Weimar Republic ended before the 1929 Depression
A sequence of political appointments and legal changes helped dismantle democracy; it was not one single election result

explanation: Hitler’s appointment and subsequent consolidation involved several political and legal steps, supported by coercion and violence.

stem: Which development followed Hitler’s appointment as chancellor in 1933?

options.text: The Nazi regime moved to suppress opposition and establish dictatorship
Germany rejoined the League and restored the monarchy
The Weimar Republic became more pluralistic
The German-Soviet Pact was signed that year

explanation: After January 1933, the Nazi government dismantled democratic institutions and consolidated dictatorial power.

stem: Which statement best describes the political outcome of Nazi consolidation?

options.text: The Reichstag gained control over the army and police
Germany became a one-party dictatorship and opposition was suppressed
The League governed Germany directly
Germany returned to the political system of 1871

explanation: The Nazi regime eliminated meaningful political competition and established a dictatorship.

stem: What did the Mukden Incident of 1931 precede?

options.text: Italy’s invasion of Ethiopia
Germany’s annexation of Austria
Japan’s expansion into Manchuria
The invasion of Poland

explanation: The Mukden Incident preceded Japan’s occupation and conquest of Manchuria.

stem: How did the League of Nations respond to Japan’s actions in Manchuria?

options.text: It sent a standing army that expelled Japan
It awarded Manchuria to Italy
It immediately dissolved the Japanese government
It investigated and criticised Japan but could not reverse the occupation

explanation: The League investigated the crisis and criticised Japan, but lacked the means and unity to reverse the occupation.

stem: Which country did Fascist Italy invade in October 1935?

options.text: Ethiopia
Austria
Czechoslovakia
Poland

explanation: Italy invaded Ethiopia in October 1935.

stem: What was one consequence of Italy’s invasion of Ethiopia for the League of Nations?

options.text: The League immediately defeated Italy militarily
The League imposed sanctions but failed to stop the conquest
Italy was given permanent control of the League
Ethiopia withdrew from the League before the invasion began

explanation: The League condemned the invasion and imposed sanctions, but these measures did not prevent Italy’s conquest.

stem: Which statement about the Spanish Civil War is accurate?

options.text: It was a war between Germany and Poland in 1939
The League’s standing army ended it in 1936
It became an international conflict in which outside powers supported opposing sides
No foreign government or volunteer took part

explanation: Foreign states and volunteers became involved on different sides; diplomatic efforts to limit intervention were contested and uneven.

stem: Which comparison between Manchuria and Ethiopia is accurate?

options.text: Both territories were annexed by Germany in 1938
The League defeated both aggressors militarily
Italy occupied Manchuria and Japan invaded Ethiopia
Japan occupied Manchuria after 1931, while Italy invaded Ethiopia in 1935; League responses failed to stop either expansion

explanation: Japan’s expansion in Manchuria and Italy’s invasion of Ethiopia exposed the League’s inability to halt aggression.

stem: What did Germany do in March 1936 in violation of the postwar settlement?

options.text: Remilitarised the Rhineland
Invaded Poland
Annexed the Sudetenland
Signed the Treaty of Versailles

explanation: German troops re-entered the demilitarised Rhineland in March 1936.

stem: What was the Anschluss of 1938?

options.text: The German occupation of the Rhineland
Germany’s annexation of Austria
The Italian invasion of Ethiopia
The Soviet invasion of Poland

explanation: The Anschluss was the annexation of Austria by Nazi Germany in March 1938.

stem: Which territory was transferred from Czechoslovakia to Germany under the Munich Agreement?

options.text: The Rhineland
Alsace-Lorraine
The Sudetenland
Danzig

explanation: The Munich Agreement of September 1938 allowed Germany to annex the Sudetenland.

stem: Which statement best describes appeasement in the 1930s?

options.text: The League used military force to remove Hitler from office
Germany agreed to disarm completely in 1938
The policy required France to join the Axis
Britain and France made concessions in an effort to avoid another war, including at Munich

explanation: British and French leaders made concessions to Hitler’s demands, hoping to preserve peace; the policy did not prevent further expansion.

stem: Which event followed the Munich Agreement of September 1938?

options.text: Germany occupied the remaining Czech lands in March 1939
Germany withdrew from Austria
The League liberated Manchuria
The Treaty of Versailles was signed

explanation: Germany occupied the rest of the Czech lands in March 1939, showing that the Munich settlement did not end expansion.

stem: Which sequence correctly orders Germany’s expansion before the invasion of Poland?

options.text: Munich Agreement → Rhineland remilitarisation → Anschluss → occupation of Czech lands
Rhineland remilitarisation → Anschluss → Munich Agreement → occupation of the rest of Czech lands
Anschluss → invasion of Poland → Rhineland remilitarisation → Munich Agreement
Occupation of Czech lands → Anschluss → Rhineland remilitarisation → Munich Agreement

explanation: Germany remilitarised the Rhineland in 1936, annexed Austria in 1938, gained the Sudetenland at Munich, and occupied the rest of the Czech lands in 1939.

stem: When did Germany and the Soviet Union sign their non-aggression pact?

options.text: June 1933
September 1931
August 1939
March 1936

explanation: Germany and the Soviet Union signed the pact in August 1939.

stem: What did the secret protocol to the German-Soviet Pact address?

options.text: The creation of the League of Nations
The transfer of Ethiopia to Italy
The disarmament of the Rhineland
The division of spheres of influence in Eastern Europe

explanation: The secret protocol divided spheres of influence in Eastern Europe, including provisions concerning Poland.

stem: On what date did Germany invade Poland in 1939?

options.text: 1 September
23 August
3 September
11 November

explanation: German forces invaded Poland on 1 September 1939.

stem: When did Britain and France declare war on Germany after the invasion of Poland?

options.text: 1 September 1939
3 September 1939
23 August 1939
30 January 1933

explanation: Britain and France declared war on Germany on 3 September 1939, after the invasion of Poland.

stem: Which sequence correctly orders the events that began the Second World War in Europe?

options.text: Invasion of Poland → German-Soviet Pact → declarations of war
Declarations of war → Pact → invasion of Poland
German-Soviet Pact → German invasion of Poland → British and French declarations of war
Pact → declarations of war → invasion of Poland

explanation: The pact was signed in August 1939, Germany invaded Poland on 1 September, and Britain and France declared war on 3 September.

stem: Which conclusion best connects the interwar crises to the outbreak of the Second World War?

options.text: The Great Depression alone caused every war in Europe
The League of Nations began the war by invading Poland
The Munich Agreement created the First World War
Economic and political instability, aggressive expansion and failed collective security interacted; no single event alone explains the wider crisis

explanation: Interwar economic crises, authoritarian politics, aggression and weak collective responses combined in the path to war; the process cannot be reduced to one cause.
